1.pericope_label: And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab. And they called the people unto the sacrifices of their gods: and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods. And Israel joined himself unto Baal–peor: and the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel. And the Lord said unto Moses, Take all the heads of the people, and hang them up before the Lord against the sun, that the fierce anger of the Lord may be turned away from Israel. And Moses said unto the judges of Israel, Slay ye every one his men that were joined unto Baal–peor.

schools.summary: Locate the camp before anything else, and explain the choice of name. Shittim is an abbreviation of Abel-Shittim, the point to which the camp of the Israelites in the steppes of Moab reached, and it is mentioned here instead of Arboth-Moab because it was at this northern limit that the Israelites came into contact with the Moabites and were invited by them to take part in their sacrificial meals; the same name is used later for the same reason, as the spot nearest the crossing of the Jordan. Then parse the verb of the opening charge. Construed with this preposition it signifies to incline to a person, to attach oneself to him so as to commit fornication, and the word applies to carnal and to spiritual whoredom alike; so the lust of the flesh induced the Israelites to approach the daughters of Moab and form friendships with them, in consequence of which they were invited to the slain-offerings of their gods, that is, to the sacrificial festivals and meals, in connection with which they also adored those gods. Identify the god as far as the evidence allows: he was worshipped in the city of Beth-peor, and is supposed to be identical with Chemosh, the Moabitish god of war. On the sentence, set out both constructions without forcing a choice. The heads or chiefs of the people seem to be identical with the judges of the following verse; some understand by all the heads only those who had been the chief offenders, while others take the verb rendered take as equivalent to assemble, or bring before thee, referring the pronoun them to the offenders. Note one thing that is certain from the next verse, that the punishment of impaling or crucifying was not to be inflicted until after death; and record that the Greek translators render the Hebrew verb used here by the same word which is elsewhere translated to put to an open shame. Finally, note that this order was not in fact carried out, because the matter took a different turn.

Begin with the moral situation rather than the geography, and state it as a general truth about the people: they were no more able to bear prosperity than adversity. Heretofore, worn out by fatigue or rendered impatient by abstinence and famine, they had often rebelled; now, having entered a habitable land and resting in the midst of fruitful fields, they are incited by their more comfortable dwellings and pleasanter mode of life to lasciviousness and the indulgence of filthy lusts. Then trace the cause back to Balaam's counsel, that the Moabites should prostitute their women in order to entice the Israelites to unholy worship; for Balaam had learnt by experience that God's favour was an invincible safeguard, and therefore invented a plan by which they might destroy themselves, depriving themselves of that protection and provoking wrath against them. Take the order of the fall seriously, since the apostle does: he refers the punishment to fornication, for although it was God's design to avenge the violation of his worship, it is fitting to examine the origin and source of the evil, as a murder committed by a drunken man is imputed to his drunkenness. Observe also that Satan creeps upon us by degrees: the Moabitish damsels did not straightway solicit the Israelites to worship their idols, but first invited them to their banquets and so tempted them to idolatry, whereas if idol-worship had been mentioned at first they might have refused. On the joining itself, note that Moses amplifies the crime by saying they bound themselves to the idol in an impious alliance, alluding to the holy union whereby God had connected himself with the people; and though it is probable that many were not impelled by superstition but merely complied with the wishes of the women, God declares them joined to the idol they only pretended to worship. Take the name simply from the mountain lately mentioned, and compare the way images are named after particular places. On the sentence, hold that the leaders were hanged while the common sort perished by pestilence, so that the more conspicuous ignominy might awaken the greater terror; and draw from it the warning that in proportion to a man's pre-eminence he has the less excuse, since obscure persons do less harm by their example.

Mark the place as an aggravation of the sin. This was their last station, from which they passed immediately into Canaan, so that they committed this when God was on the point of putting them into possession of their long-expected land. Then be careful about who the tempters were: the daughters of Moab are named, but Midian was in it too, both peoples being confederated in the wicked design, so that one is put for the other; the Moabitish women may be named because they began the transgression, or because they were the chief persons, possibly the relations or courtiers of Balak. Explain the strategy. The Moabites, being now neighbours to Israel and finding themselves unable to effect their design by war or by witchcraft, fell another way to work, contracting familiarity with them and, perceiving their evil inclinations, inviting them through their daughters to the feasts made of their portions of the sacrifices; and the participation of such a feast was reckoned a participation in the worship of the god to whom the sacrifice was offered. On the whoredom, allow both explanations: either they prostituted themselves on condition of worshipping their god, or the god himself was worshipped by such filthy acts. On the joining, note that the word implies a forsaking of the God to whom they were joined and a strict conjunction with this false one; and on the name, derive Peor either from the hill where he was worshipped or, more probably, from a verb signifying to open and uncover, because of the obscene posture in which the idol was set. Then handle the two chief conditions of the sacrifice, and do not soften them: the alliance, though contracted even in a matrimonial way, was nevertheless fornication, since no marriage between an Israelite and a Midianite could be legitimate according to the law of God. On the sentence, take the heads to be those chief both in the transgression and in place and power, singled out for exemplary punishment because their concurrence in the wickedness was the more odious and mischievous; and read against the sun as meaning publicly, since their sin was public and scandalous, and speedily, before the sun go down.

Name the strategist before the sin. Balak, by the advice of Balaam, cast this stumbling-block before the children of Israel; and note that those are our worst enemies who draw us to sin, for that is the greatest mischief any man can do us. Press the contrast that makes the story instructive: had Balak drawn out his armed men to fight them, Israel would have bravely resisted and no doubt been more than conquerors, but now that he sends his beautiful women among them and invites them to his idolatrous feasts, they basely yield and are shamefully overcome; those were smitten with his harlots who could not be smitten with his sword. From which learn the rule, that we are more endangered by the charms of a smiling world than by the terrors of a frowning world. Then observe how the two sins hang together. Whoredom and idolatry went together, for they first defiled and debauched their consciences by committing lewdness with the women, and were then easily drawn, in complaisance to them and in contempt of the God of Israel, to bow down to their idols, the more so if, as seems probable, the uncleanness was itself part of the service performed to Baal-peor. Make the general point plainly: those who have broken the fences of modesty will never be held by the bonds of piety, and those who have dishonoured themselves by fleshly lusts will not scruple to dishonour God by idolatrous worship. Add the apostle's reason against eating things offered to idols, that by eating of the idolatrous sacrifices they joined themselves to the god to whom they were offered, and that it is called eating the sacrifices of the dead not only because the idol was a dead thing but because the person represented was some hero deified after his death, as saints in the Roman church are canonized. Then finish with the aggravation of the place. It was the highest degree of treachery and ingratitude to be false to their God, whom they had found so faithful to them, and to eat of idol-sacrifices when they were ready to be feasted so richly on God's own favours, with the land of Canaan in view and just before them.

debates.question: Was the sin fornication or an unlawful marriage?

sides.position: A matrimonial alliance: both were of chief families, and the woman should not be made a common prostitute, as the Vulgate does
Corporal and spiritual whoredom together, the uncleanness being itself part of the worship of Baal-peor
Either they prostituted themselves on condition of worshipping the god, or the god was worshipped by such acts

debates.question: What does take all the heads command?

sides.position: Assemble the chiefs and judges, hold an inquiry, and hang those found guilty; against the sun means publicly and in daylight
The heads are themselves the offenders, chief in the transgression and in place and power, hanged as an example
Both constructions are open: some take the heads for the chief offenders, others read take as assemble and refer them to the offenders
Whatever it commanded, the order was never carried out, because the matter took a different turn

outliers.note: Alone reads the fall as a failure under prosperity rather than hardship: having rebelled before when worn by fatigue and famine, they are now undone by resting among fruitful fields, the easier life inciting them to lasciviousness.

Alone draws the strategic moral, that those smitten with Balak's harlots could not be smitten with his sword, and that we are more endangered by the charms of a smiling world than by the terrors of a frowning one.

6.pericope_label: And, behold, one of the children of Israel came and brought unto his brethren a Midianitish woman in the sight of Moses, and in the sight of all the congregation of the children of Israel, who were weeping before the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. And when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, and took a javelin in his hand; And he went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel, and the woman through her belly. So the plague was stayed from the children of Israel. And those that died in the plague were twenty and four thousand.

schools.summary: Fix the moment precisely, because the timing is the enormity. Whilst the heads of the people were deliberating on the subject, and the whole congregation was assembled before the tabernacle weeping on account of the divine wrath, there came an Israelite, a prince of the tribe of Simeon, who brought a Midianitish woman, the daughter of a Midianitish chief, to his brethren, that is, into the camp of the Israelites, before the eyes of Moses and all the congregation. This shameless wickedness, in which the depth of the corruption that had penetrated into the congregation came to light, inflamed the zeal of Phinehas, so that he seized a spear and, rushing into the tent, pierced both of them through in the very act. Then handle the rare word for the place. It occurs only here; it means literally the arched, and may refer to the inner or hinder part of the ordinary tent, which was occupied by the women, or it may denote an arched or vaulted tent, probably of skins, erected while the Israelites were joining with the Moabites and Midianites in the worship of Baal-peor. Record what the versions made of it, the Greek a furnace and the Latin a brothel, and add that the phrase rendered through her belly may equally be within her tent, some thinking that the word which occurs earlier in the verse stands there a second time. On the description of Phinehas, press the punctuation: the designation the priest, which generally denotes the high priest, refers to Aaron and not to Phinehas, since Eleazar was high priest at this time, though Phinehas was invested with civil as well as ecclesiastical authority. Say what the act accomplished: through this judgment the plague was restrained, and the example made of these sinners was an act of intercession by which the wrath of God was appeased, the punishment inflicted as a purifying chastisement serving as a covering against the exterminating judgment. On the numbers, note that the apostle gives twenty-three thousand where Moses gives twenty-four, probably from a traditional interpretation which deducted the thousand hanged by the judges; or, presuming no error of the scribes, the words in one day may account for the difference.

Say at once that this case was foul and detestable beyond others. There is no doubt that many, amid such gross licentiousness as had for some time prevailed, had filled the camp with scandalous offences; but there was something peculiarly enormous in this act, in that an impious despiser of God wantonly insulted both God and men amidst the tears and lamentations of all, as if triumphing over shame and modesty. The multitude were weeping before the tabernacle, that is, all the pious who trembled at the thought of approaching calamity, being fully persuaded that this licentiousness, accompanied by idolatry and sacrilege, would not go unpunished; and meanwhile this abandoned man rushes forward and, in mockery of their tears, leads his harlot in procession. Observe next that the order of the history is inverted, since it is not credible that after the judges had begun to perform their office such an iniquity should have been committed; the narrative is inserted here in order to make it more apparent how necessary it was to proceed speedily to severe chastisement. Then celebrate the courage of Phinehas, who, while the rest were hesitating, inflamed with holy zeal, hastened forward to inflict punishment; and condemn the backwardness of the others by implication, though their tears were praiseworthy, since being almost stupefied by grief their virtue was not clear of all defect. Face the objection squarely. If any say that he transgressed the limits of his calling when he laid hold of the sword with which God had not armed him, reply that our calling is not always confined to its ordinary office, inasmuch as God sometimes requires new and unusual acts of his servants; as a priest it was not the office of Phinehas to punish crime, but he was called by the special inspiration of God, so that in his private capacity he had the Holy Spirit as his guide. Then set the fence around it that the passage requires: these circumstances ought not to be regarded as an example, so that a general rule may be laid down from them, and if any private person should in his preposterous zeal take upon himself to punish a similar crime, in vain will he boast that he is an imitator of Phinehas unless he is thoroughly assured of the command of God. Let the answer of Christ always be borne in mind, whereby he restrained his disciples when they desired that fire should come down from heaven: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. On the numbers, allow that the exact account is not always observed, and that the apostle, subtracting one thousand, was content with the lesser; from which we may perceive how severe and terrible the punishment was, and learn to beware of provoking God by fornication.

Settle who these two people were before judging the act, since their rank changes what the act was. Zimri was the son of Salu, a prince of a chief family in the tribe of Simeon; Cozbi was the daughter of Zur, head over a people of one of the chief families in Midian. The condition of these two persons plainly proves it to have been a matrimonial alliance, the one a prince and the other a princess; therefore fornication in the common sense of the word was not practised on this occasion. The matter was bad enough, since the marriage was in flat opposition to the law of God, and we need not make it worse by representing the woman as a common prostitute, as the Vulgate and several others have done; in such a case that is absolutely inadmissible, and Josephus says positively that Zimri had married Cozbi. Then mark the aggravation of the timing: this was done when Moses had given the charge to the judges and, as it seems, before the execution of it, since otherwise the man would not have been so foolish as to run upon certain ruin when the examples were frequent before his eyes; and to do it in the sight of Moses argues intolerable impudence and contempt of God, while the people were bewailing the wickedness and imploring God's mercy. On the act of Phinehas, be careful to make it lawful rather than heroic in the wrong sense. He was himself a man in great authority, and did this after the command given by Moses to the rulers to slay these transgressors, and in the very sight and no doubt by the consent of Moses himself, and also by the special direction of God's Spirit; he was inspired undoubtedly by the Spirit of the God of justice to do an act which can never be a precedent on any common occasion. Illustrate that from later history if it helps, comparing a magistrate whose sudden act of zeal was of essential benefit at the time and justified only by the pressing exigencies of the case. On the numbers, reconcile them by counting: a thousand men were slain in consequence of the examination first instituted, and twenty-three thousand in consequence of the orders that followed, making twenty-four thousand in the whole, while the apostle probably refers only to the latter number; both sorts, however, may be said to have died of the plague, the word being used, as often it is, for the stroke or hand of God.

Frame the whole passage as a contest between wickedness and righteousness, which shall be the more bold and resolute; and say at the outset that righteousness carries the day, as no doubt it will at last. Then take the wickedness first. Never was vice more daring than in Zimri, a prince of a chief house in Simeon, who had arrived at such a degree of impudence that he publicly appeared leading a Midianitish harlot, and a harlot of quality like himself, in the sight of Moses and all the good people of Israel. He did not think it enough to go out with her to worship the gods of Moab, but when he had done that he brought her back to dishonour the God of Israel; he owned her publicly as higher in his favour than any daughter of Israel, and openly went with her into a booth designed and fitted up for lewdness. Thus he declared his sin as Sodom, and was so far from blushing for it that he rather gloried in his shame. Number the circumstances that made it exceedingly sinful. It was an affront to the justice of the nation and bade defiance to it, for the judges were ordered to put the criminals to death and he thought himself too great for them to meddle with, in effect bidding them touch him if they durst; he had certainly cast off all fear of God who stood in no awe of the powers God had ordained to be a terror to evil-doers. And it was an affront to the religion of the nation, for Moses and the main body of the congregation, who kept their integrity, were weeping at the door of the tabernacle, sanctifying a fast in a solemn assembly to turn away the wrath of God; and then comes Zimri among them with his harlot in his hand to banter them, and in effect to tell them that he was resolved to fill the measure of sin as fast as they emptied it. Then take the righteousness. Never was virtue more daring than in Phinehas, who rose up from his prayers, took his half-pike, followed the sinners into the tent and stabbed them both. Justify him carefully and narrowly: being now heir-apparent to the high-priesthood, he was doubtless one of the judges Moses had ordered by divine appointment to slay those who had joined themselves to Baal-peor, so that this gives no countenance to private persons who, under pretence of zeal against sin, would put offenders to death when they ought to be prosecuted by due course of law; the civil magistrate is the avenger, and no private person may take his work out of his hand.

debates.question: What was the tent Zimri took her into?

sides.position: A vessel-shaped booth: the Aruch makes it narrow above and broad below, a place where whores were put, and the Talmud uses it for a brothel
Either the inner part of a common tent where the women lodged, or an arched tent of skins put up for the worship of Baal-peor
The arched or hinder part of the tent
A booth designed and fitted up for lewdness

debates.question: May the act of Phinehas be imitated?

sides.position: No: he was inspired by the Spirit of the God of justice, and it can never be a precedent on any common occasion
No, and no special inspiration is needed to explain it: as heir to the high priesthood he was one of the judges already commanded to kill the offenders
No: a calling is not always confined to its ordinary office, but this was special inspiration and not a rule — ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of

debates.question: Twenty-four thousand, or the apostle's twenty-three?

sides.position: A thousand were hanged and the rest fell by the plague; the apostle counts only those that fell
The exact account of numbers is not always observed; the apostle was content with the lesser, round figure
Presuming no scribal error, the apostle's words in one day may account for the difference

outliers.note: Alone illustrates the act from English history, comparing the mayor of London striking down Wat Tyler at Smithfield — the act of a zealot, of essential benefit at the time and justified only by the pressing exigency.

Alone argues that the narrative stands out of chronological order, since it is not credible the offence was committed after the judges had begun their work, and that it is placed here to show how urgently severe chastisement was needed.

10.pericope_label: And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, hath turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy. Wherefore say, Behold, I give unto him my covenant of peace: And he shall have it, and his seed after him, even the covenant of an everlasting priesthood; because he was zealous for his God, and made an atonement for the children of Israel.

schools.summary: Get the possessive right first, since the whole commendation rests on it. The phrase is not zeal for me but my zeal, the zeal of Jehovah with which Phinehas was filled and by which he was impelled to put the daring sinners to death; better rendered, in that he was jealous with my jealousy, or, in that he displayed my jealousy. By doing this he had averted destruction from the Israelites and restrained the working of Jehovah's zeal, which had manifested itself in the plague. Note next why the genealogy is repeated in full, exactly as it stood two verses earlier: it is repeated as if to denote that he was not a private individual but one invested with public authority. Then take the grant in its own legal terms. To give a covenant is to fulfil it, to grant what was promised in it; and the covenant granted to Phinehas consisted in this, that an eternal priesthood, that is, the eternal possession of the priesthood, was secured to him and to his descendants after him as a covenant, that is, in an irrevocable form, since God never breaks a covenant he has made. Trace the history of that grant honestly, including its interruptions. Phinehas succeeded his father Eleazar as high priest; there was a temporary interruption in the succession in the time of Eli, continuing until the time of David, when there appears to have been a joint high-priesthood; the office was restored by Solomon to Zadok, the descendant of Phinehas, and so continued until the gradual dissolution of the Jewish state. Then read the covenant forward. The covenant of grace is itself described by the prophets as a covenant of peace, and Phinehas, zealous for the honour of God and of the house of the Lord, was a fitting type of him in whom the psalmist's word was accomplished, the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; so the covenant made by the blood of the cross, and all the blessings belonging to it, stand fast with Christ and are secured to his spiritual seed, whose priesthood is an unchangeable priesthood, a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.

Show first that God makes himself the author of the deaths, not only because he was thus propitiated toward the people, but because he calls the zeal of Phinehas his own. The words will bear taking either actively or passively, that Phinehas was inflamed with zeal to vindicate God's glory, or that he took upon him the zeal of God himself; whichever is preferred, God refers to himself what was done by Phinehas. Then guard the language of appeasement against abuse, for it is the point at which this text is most often misused. When God declares that he was appeased by the punishment inflicted, let us not imagine that there was a meritorious satisfaction of the sort by which the Papists feign that their punishments are redeemed before God; for although the just chastisements of sin are sacrifices of sweet savour, they are by no means expiations to reconcile God. There is no question here of compensation: what is meant is that it was a means of appeasing God when the ungodliness of the people, which had as it were fanned up his wrath into a flame, was repressed by this severe correction. Confirm it from the psalm, where the atonement is ascribed not to the act of Phinehas but to his prayer, because in right of his priesthood he had humbly interceded for the people; and add the apostle's rule, that those are not judged by God who voluntarily judge themselves, since by their penitence they in a manner prevent the judgment. Then meet the objection about the reward. If any say that Phinehas obtained nothing new, since by the rule of the law he was the undoubted successor of his father, reply that it is not uncommon that what God had already freely promised he declares he will give by way of reward, as the blessing promised to Abraham before the birth of Isaac is repeated after he was prepared to sacrifice him. Add that the privilege of a single individual is not simply in question, but a perpetual succession, as if God had promised that his posterity should never fail; and that the change at the commencement of Solomon's reign is not repugnant to the promise, since it may probably be inferred that Zadok no less than Abiathar was of the race of Phinehas. Take the covenant of peace to mean a covenant surely established, indicating prosperity, as if God had said that Phinehas and his posterity should prosperously execute the sacerdotal office. And observe finally that his descent is recorded partly to show that he was no private person but a man of public authority, perhaps one of the very judges Moses had ordered to slay, and partly to show that he was heir apparent to the priesthood, which this action should not hinder but rather confirm to him.

Explain the phrase covenant of peace from two directions at once. It is the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, as the next verse expounds it, and it is called a covenant of peace partly with respect to the happy effect of this heroical action, whereby he made peace between God and his people, and partly with regard to the principal end of the priestly office itself, which was constantly to do what Phinehas had now done: to mediate between God and men, to obtain and preserve his own and Israel's reconciliation with God by offering sacrifices and incense and prayers on their behalf, and also by turning men away from iniquity, which is the only peace-breaker, and by pressing the observation of that law which is the only bond of peace. Allow that the word peace, implying all kinds of blessing both spiritual and temporal, may also mean no more here than a promise to grant him and his family the utmost prosperity in reference to both worlds. Then be exact about how far the everlasting priesthood extends, and do not overstate it. Taken of the Mosaic dispensation, it was to continue as long as the law and commonwealth of the Jews did; but that promise was conditional, and therefore might be made void by the miscarriages of Phinehas's sons, as it seems it was, whereupon a like promise was made to Eli of the line of Ithamar, that he and his should walk before the Lord for ever, which also for his and their sins was made void, and the priesthood returned to Phinehas's line in the time of Solomon. Taken properly, however, the everlasting priesthood refers to the priesthood of Christ, which was shadowed out by the priesthood under the law, no matter in what family it was continued; the priesthood alone is everlasting, and a grant of that was made to Phinehas and his descendants. Count the succession for the reader, since the reckoning is instructive: twelve high priests of the race of Phinehas from this time to the days of Solomon, nine more from that time to the captivity, and fifteen from the return to the time of Antiochus Eupator; the family of Ithamar held the priesthood for about a hundred and fifty years, but it was restored to the family of Phinehas in the person of Zadok, in which it continued in the whole about nine hundred and fifty years.

sides.position: Not zeal for me but my zeal — the jealousy of Jehovah with which Phinehas was filled
Either reading will serve, active or passive; on both God claims the deed as his own

debates.question: How long does the everlasting priesthood run?

sides.position: As long as the law and commonwealth of the Jews; but the promise was conditional and was made void, then restored under Solomon
It refers properly to the priesthood of Christ, no matter what family held the office
Through an interruption under Eli and a joint priesthood under David to Zadok, and forward to Christ's unchangeable priesthood
There was no real break: Zadok no less than Abiathar was probably of the race of Phinehas
An eternal possession secured in irrevocable form, since God never breaks a covenant he has made

outliers.note: Alone guards the word atonement against a doctrine of merit, denying that the punishment was a satisfaction and pointing to the psalm, where the atonement is ascribed not to the act of Phinehas but to his prayer.

Alone counts the whole succession — twelve high priests of this race to Solomon, nine more to the captivity, fifteen after the return — and reckons the line held the office some nine hundred and fifty years in all.

14.pericope_label: Now the name of the Israelite that was slain, even that was slain with the Midianitish woman, was Zimri, the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites. And the name of the Midianitish woman that was slain was Cozbi, the daughter of Zur; he was head over a people, and of a chief house in Midian. And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Vex the Midianites, and smite them: For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, which was slain in the day of the plague for Peor's sake.

schools.summary: Correct the two titles from the Hebrew before drawing anything from them. A prince of a chief house among the Simeonites is better rendered of a father's house; and the description of Zur, head over a people and of a chief house in Midian, is better read as head of the tribes, or communities, of a father's house in Midian, several of the Midianitish tribes or smaller divisions of a father's house having perhaps descended from one tribe-father. Note that Zur appears again in the later narrative as one of the five kings of Midian slain by the Israelites. Draw the probable inference about the tribe: Simeon seems to have been deeply implicated in the transgression, and those who belonged to it were likely the chief sufferers in the plague, which the census figures in the following chapter bear out. Then state the ground of the command against Midian: the Lord now commanded Moses to show hostility to the Midianites and to smite them, on account of the stratagem they had practised upon the Israelites in tempting them to idolatry. Explain why they and not their confederates. The Midianites appear to have been joint actors with the Moabites throughout the whole opposition offered to Israel, and the chief actors in the wiles by which Israel was seduced; and as descendants of Abraham, the father of the faithful, they ought to have feared and obeyed Abraham's God and shown brotherly kindness to his people, who were their own kindred. Observe that the special judgments of God are directed against the sins of apostasy and of seduction. Then correct a common explanation of the exemption of Moab. They were not to be smitten with the Midianites, but they did not escape punishment, being shut out, even to the tenth generation, from the congregation of the Lord; and their exemption at this time was probably due not to their descent from Lot, since the Midianites were themselves descended from Abraham, but to the fact that the measure of their sin was not yet full.

Say why the two names are recorded at all. As the memory of the just is blessed, so it was equitable that the author of this foul sin should be condemned to perpetual infamy. Notice then that part of the disgrace is thrown upon the whole tribe, which shows how greatly displeasing to God this gross enormity was; for although the tribe of Simeon is not actually involved in the charge of participating in the sin, they are all branded with the common mark of ignominy for their humiliation, in order that each of them may learn severely to correct whomsoever among his relatives he sees offending, and by no means to encourage their vices, if he desires to do credit to the founder of his race; for that is the true way to honour one's family and blood. Take the rank of both parties as teaching two things at once: that God's judgment is no respecter of persons, in that it does not spare rank, and that the higher a person is in position the greater the disgrace to which he is exposed if he conduct himself dishonourably, since their very dignity renders men's actions more conspicuous. Where the evidence gives out, stop: because the paternal house of the woman is said to have been in Midian, some conjecture she was born in Moab or brought up there among her maternal relatives, but as the matter is unimportant, leave it undecided. On the war, meet the difficulty that God constantly forbids his people to take vengeance, so that it is surprising to see them now instigated to it. Bear in mind that God, who is the just avenger of all wickedness, often makes use of men's instrumentality and constitutes them the lawful ministers of his vengeance, so that vengeance must not be condemned without exception, but only such as men are impelled to by carnal passions: if a man is carried to it by the stimulus of his own private injury, that is manifestly wrong, but if he is led to inflict punishment by a just and well-regulated zeal towards God, it is not his own cause but God's that he undertakes. God did not therefore give reins to his people's anger, but armed them with his own sword. And where the delay in punishing Moab cannot be explained, say so: no good reason appears why God should mercifully bear with the one nation while hastening to punish the other, so let us learn to regard his judgments with reverence and not presume to discuss them further than is lawful. It is enough to know that war was justly declared against the Midianites, because it was not their fault that Israel was not ruined by the impiety to which they induced them.

Ask why the Midianites and not the Moabites, and answer from their conduct rather than their pedigree. It is probable the Midianites were the most guilty: in persuading Balak to send for Balaam, in the reception of Balaam after Balak had dismissed him, in further consultation with him, and in contriving the means for executing this wicked plot. Then explain the word wiles, which is the hinge of the charge. They vexed Israel not with wars but with wiles, with cunning stratagems and artful methods to draw them into sin, that thereby they might be exposed to the wrath of God; for under pretence of kindred and friendship and leagues, which they offered instead of the war the Israelites expected, they sought only an opportunity to insinuate themselves into their familiarity and execute their plot of bringing that curse upon Israel which they had in vain attempted to bring another way. Be specific about the means: they beguiled Israel by sending their daughters among them, and in the matter of Cozbi by prostituting a person of such quality to a prince of theirs, which was setting an example for the other daughters of Midian to follow, so that many were ensnared into whoredom and thence into idolatry. Note the idiom by which she is called their sister, since it was common with eastern people to call those of the same country their brethren and sisters. Then point forward to the execution of the order, so that the reader sees it carried out: twelve thousand Israelites attacked the Midianites, destroyed all their cities, slew their five kings and every male and every grown-up woman, and took all their spoils. And close by naming what the command teaches now, since a merely historical reading would waste it: whatever draws us to sin should be a vexation to us, and God will certainly reckon with those who do the devil's work in tempting men to sin.

Distinguish the two punishments, since the distinction is the point of the section. God punished the Israelites for their sin with a plague; as a Father he corrected his own children with a rod. But we do not read that any of the Midianites died of the plague: God took another course with them, and punished them with the sword of an enemy, not with the rod of a father. Observe next who is charged with the execution. Moses, though the meekest man, and far from a spirit of revenge, is the one ordered to vex the Midianites and smite them; from which learn that we must set ourselves against that, whatever it is, which is an occasion of sin to us, though it be a right eye or a right hand that thus offends us. Call that by its proper name: it is the holy indignation and revenge which godly sorrow worketh. Then give the reason the text itself gives for the order, that they vex you with their wiles, and turn it into the rule the passage exists to teach: whatever draws us to sin should be a vexation to us, as a thorn in the flesh. Weigh the two kinds of injury against each other, and refuse to rank the subtler one lower. The mischief which the Midianites did to Israel by enticing them to whoredom must be remembered and punished with as much severity as that which the Amalekites did in fighting with them when they came out of Egypt. God will certainly reckon with those that do the devil's work in tempting men to sin.

outliers.note: Alone explains why the disgrace touches the whole tribe of Simeon, which was not itself charged: each man is branded so that he may learn to correct any offending relative, that being the true way to honour his own blood.

Alone contrasts the two punishments as different instruments, Israel corrected with a father's rod in the plague while Midian was punished with the sword of an enemy, no Midianite being said to have died of the plague.
